narration: A crowd of penguins stands at the edge of the ice. They're hungry, and the fish are right there, below them. But not one of them moves.
They shuffle. They lean forward. They step back again. They're waiting for someone else to go first, because somewhere in that dark water, something may be waiting too.
It's long, it's silver, and it's patient. Meet the leopard seal, the top hunter of the Antarctic coast, and one of the strangest predators on the planet.
In this video, we'll find out how it's built, what it eats, why penguins fear it, how it sings, and what really happens when it meets people.

The leopard seal's scientific name is Hydrurga leptonyx. It's a true seal, part of the same family as harbor seals and elephant seals. That means it has no ear flaps, just small openings on the side of its head.
It lives mostly in the pack ice that surrounds Antarctica, a vast and shifting world of floating ice that grows every winter and shrinks every summer.
And the name? It comes from its coat. A leopard seal is silver-gray on top, paler underneath, and covered in dark spots, a little like a big cat.
Leopard seals are big. The largest reach around 3.5 meters, about 11 feet, and can weigh close to half a ton. That's roughly as heavy as seven grown men.
And here's the twist. In many animals, males are the bigger sex. With leopard seals, it's the other way around. The biggest leopard seals are females.
Then there's the head. It's enormous for a seal, with a long snout and a wide mouth that stretches back past the eyes. Some people say it looks almost like a reptile.
Most true seals swim by sweeping their back flippers side to side. Leopard seals often power through the water with their long front flippers instead, almost like wings.
Their bodies are slender and flexible, which makes them fast and agile. They can twist, turn and accelerate in a burst, exactly what you need when your prey is a quick, slippery penguin.
Most of their dives are fairly shallow, but they can hold their breath for many minutes when they need to.
Now let's look inside that mouth, because it hides one of nature's neatest tricks. At the front are long, sharp canine teeth, perfect for grabbing and holding prey.
But further back are the cheek teeth. Each one has three sharp points. When the jaws close, those points lock together and leave tiny gaps between them, like the holes in a kitchen strainer.
That lets a leopard seal take a big gulp of water full of krill, the tiny shrimp-like animals that swarm in the Southern Ocean, and then push the water back out while the krill stay inside.
Think about that. The same animal that hunts penguins can also feed a little like a whale. One mouth, two completely different ways to eat.
So what does a leopard seal actually eat? Pretty much whatever the season offers. Krill can make up a big part of the diet at certain times of the year. Fish and squid are on the menu too.
Then there are the penguins. A penguin is fast underwater, but a leopard seal only has to win once.
And leopard seals also hunt other seals, especially young ones. Many crabeater seals carry long scars on their bodies, thought to come from leopard seal attacks they survived when they were young.
Leopard seals can't chew big prey into small bites. So with a large catch, they often shake it hard at the surface to tear it into pieces they can swallow.
The leopard seal's favorite weapon is patience. It often lingers close to the ice edge, right where penguins have to enter and leave the water.
It can wait quietly near the surface, hard to spot from above. To a penguin standing on the ice, the water may look completely empty.
That's why penguins hesitate. And when they finally jump, they often go together. A crowd of birds splashing in at once is much harder to target than one penguin alone.
The same danger waits on the way home. Coming back out of the water, penguins often launch themselves onto the ice as fast as they can.
Here's something most people never hear. Leopard seals sing.
During the breeding season, males produce long, low, eerie calls underwater, repeating them again and again. To human ears, they sound almost like something from science fiction.
Scientists record these songs with underwater microphones. Because leopard seals are so hard to find and count, listening to them is one of the best ways to learn where they are.
Leopard seals are mostly loners. You'll usually see them alone, resting on an ice floe between hunts.
Females give birth on the pack ice, usually in the southern summer. The pup nurses for a few weeks, then has to learn to hunt for itself.
As adults, leopard seals have very few natural enemies. Killer whales are the main one.
In the wild, leopard seals can live for more than two decades.
People have been meeting leopard seals for a long time. In 1916, during Ernest Shackleton's famous expedition, the crew were camped on drifting sea ice after their ship was crushed.
One crew member, Thomas Orde-Lees, was chased across the ice by a leopard seal. Another expedition member shot the animal before it could reach him.
Today, divers and scientists meet leopard seals far more often. And most of those encounters are about curiosity. The seal circles, watches, opens its mouth, and eventually swims away.
Some are downright strange. One wildlife photographer described a female that kept bringing him penguins, again and again, as if she was trying to feed him.

But leopard seals are powerful wild predators, and that should never be forgotten. In 2003, a leopard seal killed British marine biologist Kirsty Brown while she was snorkeling near her research station.
It's the only known human death caused by the species. It led to stricter safety rules for scientists working in Antarctic waters, including closer watch for seals before anyone enters the water.
Leopard seals don't always stay in the far south. Young seals in particular sometimes wander thousands of kilometers north.
They've turned up on the coasts of New Zealand, Australia, South America and South Africa. In New Zealand, they're now seen often enough that some are treated as residents rather than rare visitors.
When a leopard seal hauls out on a busy beach, the advice is simple: give it plenty of space, and keep dogs well away.
Studying an animal that lives scattered across a frozen ocean is hard work. Researchers often start by simply searching for seals resting on the ice, from boats, ships and aircraft.
Some leopard seals have been fitted with small tags that track where they travel and how deep they dive. When the seal molts, the tag falls off with the old fur.
Others have carried tiny cameras, giving scientists a seal's-eye view of how it searches, chases and catches its food.
And some of the best clues are hiding in what the seals leave behind. By studying their droppings, scientists can identify bones, beaks and even DNA from the animals they ate.
Leopard seals have a scary reputation, so let's clear up a few myths.
Myth number one: leopard seals mostly eat penguins. In reality, their diet changes with the season and the place. Krill, fish and other seals can matter just as much.
Myth number two: every leopard seal that approaches a diver is attacking. Most are curious. But because a real attack can come without warning, divers still treat every encounter seriously.
And myth number three: leopard seals and polar bears might meet. They never do. Polar bears live in the Arctic, at the top of the planet. Leopard seals live in the Antarctic, at the bottom.
Leopard seals depend on sea ice. They rest on it, give birth on it, and molt on it. And their food web depends on it too, especially the krill that so many Antarctic animals rely on.
In recent years, Antarctic sea ice has reached some of its lowest levels on record. Scientists are watching closely to understand what that means for animals like the leopard seal.
The surprising part? Nobody knows exactly how many leopard seals there are. They live scattered across a huge, icy ocean, which makes them one of the hardest seals on Earth to count.
So the next time you see penguins hesitating at the edge of the ice, you'll know why. They're not being shy. They're being smart.
The leopard seal isn't a monster. It's a brilliant, flexible hunter, built for one of the harshest places on Earth.
